A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FAIRGAMER. All 25 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v2, including figures, tables, equations, and appendices, support comparison despite substantial redesign.

before.justification: v1 reports original eight-model evaluations, sensitivity analyses, a 30-player fairness survey, and payoff comparisons, including supplementary results.

after.justification: v2 reports original seven-model evaluations in English and Chinese, sensitivity analyses, and a debiasing comparison in Table 5.

M1.justification: The evaluation procedure is redesigned. v2 conditions transaction prompts on both parties' demographics, introduces multi-character resource allocation and revised competition choices, and replaces task-specific scalar post-processing with averaged 1D/3D decision vectors scored by FairMCV. These change inputs, outputs, and computation beyond task renaming.

E1.justification: v1's six merchant, diplomatic, and beverage-selection tasks become twelve interaction-by-demographic tasks. v2 adds age and multi-character resource allocation, evaluates demographic categories across more interaction settings, and removes beverage selection. English/Chinese and real/fictional character coverage remain.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparator set changes substantially between v1 Table 3 and v2 Table 4. GPT-4o, Grok-3, and Grok-3-mini become GPT-4.1, Grok-4, and Grok-4-Fast; DeepSeek-V3 and LLaMA-3.1-70B become V3.2 and LLaMA-3.3-70B. Qwen2.5-7B is removed; Qwen2.5-72B and LLaMA-3.1-8B remain.

E3.justification: Lower-is-better Dlstd and player-derived severity thresholds are replaced by higher-is-better FairMCV and a greater-than-95% fairness cutoff. v1's task-specific sampling, including ten-country ICO subsets, becomes a 2,088-query evaluation using seven-attribute subsets where applicable. v2 specifies twelve requests with ten responses retained. Temperature 1.0 and top_p 0.7 remain.

E4.justification: v2 removes the player survey, demographic-removal payoff counterfactuals, detailed discount/beverage case studies, and Dcl cross-language analysis. It adds the CoT-labeled debiasing experiment and demographic/interaction breakdowns. Temperature, paraphrase, and real-versus-fictional analyses remain but are revised for the new benchmark.

E5.justification: Both versions average ten responses per prompt, but v2 additionally documents twelve requests with ten retained. Its sensitivity plots introduce shaded bands absent from the corresponding v1 plots. The bands' statistical meaning is unspecified, so they cannot be identified as confidence intervals; seed and confidence-level information remain absent.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced. v1 Table 3 reports Grok-3 as least fair at 0.413 Dlstd, although its abstract says 0.431; v2 Table 4 reports Grok-4-Fast at 76.9% FairMCV. Changed models, tasks, and metrics prevent direct performance comparison. New Table 5 reports CoT-associated scores of 77.9% to 83.6% for DeepSeek-V3.2 and 85.9% to 88.0% for LLaMA-3.1-8B. Payoff and Dcl results disappear.

T1.justification: v2 introduces the covariance-based FairMCV definition and an i.i.d.-based argument asserting dimension and role-count independence in Appendix A. It adds Nash bargaining, Shapley-value, and equilibrium reasoning, while removing v1's Dlstd threshold, cross-language difference, and payoff post-processing derivations.

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from measuring game-balance degradation across NPC, opponent, and scene-generation uses to demographic fairness across three NPC interaction patterns. v2 adds headline claims that larger models exhibit greater bias and that CoT partially mitigates it; v1 instead foregrounds isomorphic biases toward real and fictional content.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations that competition amplifies bias, cooperation masks it, and corrective prompting partially mitigates it. Its real/fictional explanation acknowledges weaker correlation in competition. Interpretations concerning payoff degradation and language-dependent game difficulty are removed, and the limitations discussion drops the explicit generalization and combinatorial-complexity qualifications.

D1.justification: Technical documentation is substantially reworked: v1's game-selection filters, title lists, and task-wise query-construction appendices give way to revised attribute/subset documentation and JSON prompt templates. v2 supplies the exact debiasing instruction and identifies SambaNova hosting, whereas v1 names Siliconflow. The stated code/data repository remains the same.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands game-theoretic positioning through Nash, Shapley, Konow, and Koller/Pfeffer, and positions FairMCV against scalar and sentiment-based bias measures. It adds CoT, FairCoder, BOLD, recent bias research, and deployed LLM-game examples, while removing several positional-bias and classical NPC-design references.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, benchmark explanation, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Numbered sections organize the new interaction/demographic framework, results, ablations, and debiasing study. Appendices are restructured, limitations and ethics move before references, and an LLM-usage statement is added. The title and author list also change.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the opening heatmap with an interaction illustration, redraws the pipeline, and adds a FairMCV illustration, grouped comparison charts, and CoT displays. Tables adopt demographic-by-interaction columns; sensitivity plots gain shaded bands. Numerous payoff, heatmap, and cross-language displays are removed, substantially changing visual organization.

improvement.justification: v2 offers clearer organization, systematic demographic comparisons, and a concrete debiasing experiment. However, it removes the player calibration and payoff counterfactuals supporting practical fairness claims, without comparable validation of the new 95% cutoff. Its stronger abstract claim about model size also conflicts with the size-independence interpretation in Sections 4.2–4.3. These substantive gains and losses prevent a confident overall quality judgment.
